question: How do light-dependent reactions provide the energy carriers used by the Calvin cycle?

actual_final_response.answer_text: The light-dependent reactions use certain molecules, called energy carriers, to temporarily store energy, and these carriers move energy from the light-dependent reactions to the light-independent reactions [ev_005]. Photosystems absorb light and use electron transport chains to convert energy into the chemical energy of ATP and NADH, as this passage states [ev_002]. The overall purpose of the light-dependent reactions is to convert light energy into chemical energy, and this chemical energy will be used by the Calvin cycle to fuel the assembly of sugar molecules [ev_008]. The energy-carrying molecules ATP and NADPH travel into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle reactions take place [ev_007]. The carriers that move energy from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle are described as "full" because they bring energy; after the energy is released, the "empty" carriers return to the light-dependent reactions to obtain more energy [ev_001]. In the Calvin cycle, the energy in ATP and NADPH is used to convert three-carbon molecules into G3P [ev_010].
actual_final_response.short_answer: Light-dependent reactions capture light energy in ATP and NADPH, which move to the stroma to power the Calvin cycle [ev_002] [ev_007].
